title: Application to vacate the order issued by the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit

pages.text:
No. 25 __
In the Supreme Court of the United States
───────────
KATHERINE A. LONDON, ESQ., APPLICANT
v.
 UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS FOR THE SEVENTH CIRCUIT
───────────
APPLICATION TO VACATE THE ORDER ISSUED
BY THE UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS FOR THE SEVENTH 
CIRCUIT AND REQUEST FOR AN IMMEDIATE ADMINISTRATIVE 
STAY
───────────
KATHERINE A. LONDON, Esq.
Pro Se
 KMFL Law, Inc.
 100 Illinois St. Suite 200
 St. Charles, IL 60174
 klondon@kmfllaw.com

JURISDICTIONAL STATEMENT
This Court has jurisdiction over this application pursuant to the All Writs 
Act, 28 U.S.C. § 1651(a), which empowers the Supreme Court and its Justices 
to "issue all writs necessary or appropriate in aid of their respective 
jurisdictions and agreeable to the usages and principles of law." The application 
seeks vacatur of the Seventh Circuit's November 7, 2025, sanction order in 
Butler v. Eddi et al., No. 25-2589, or, alternatively, an immediate 
administrative stay of its enforcement, including the $750 fine (due December 
7, 2025), public reprimand, and referral to the Illinois Attorney Registration 
and Disciplinary Commission (ARDC). The underlying order arises from an 
interlocutory appeal in a federal Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt 
Organizations Act (RICO) action, over which this Court exercises supervisory 
authority to ensure due process, protect First Amendment rights in advocacy, 
and prevent abuses of discretion by lower federal courts.
This application is properly brought under Rules 22 and 23 of the Rules of 
this Court. Rule 22 permits an applicant to seek extraordinary relief directly 
from an individual Justice, typically the Circuit Justice assigned to the relevant 
court of appeals, for matters requiring prompt intervention, such as stays, 
injunctions, or vacaturs to avert irreparable harm. Here, the application is 
addressed to Justice Amy Coney Barrett, the Circuit Justice for the Seventh 
Circuit, who has the authority to grant the requested relief independently. This 
procedure facilitates expeditious resolution of urgent issues without 
necessitating initial review by the full Court, as evidenced by this Court's 
practice in cases involving imminent enforcement of sanctions, threats to 
ongoing litigation, or risks to public safety (e.g., stays in execution or 
enforcement contexts). An individual Justice may issue such relief under the 
All Writs Act to preserve the status quo pending further proceedings.
In contrast, a petition for a writ of mandamus under Rule 20 is generally 
directed to the full Court and serves as a vehicle to compel a lower court to 
perform a mandatory duty or rectify a clear abuse of discretion where no other 
adequate remedy exists. Mandamus is an extraordinary remedy reserved for 
final disposition on the merits, often after exhaustion of other avenues, and 
typically requires collective consideration by the Justices. While mandamus 
could ultimately address the substantive validity of the Seventh Circuit's order, 
such as its alleged violations of due process, First Amendment protections for 
zealous advocacy, and Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 46, this Rule 22 
application is specifically designed for interim relief. It enables a single Justice 
to act swiftly on time-sensitive elements like the impending fine and 
disciplinary referral, which pose immediate and irreparable harm to 
Applicant's professional standing, client representation, and the safety of 
vulnerable individuals in the underlying RICO case. If granted, such relief

would not preclude subsequent mandamus proceedings but would safeguard 
Applicant's rights during the interim.
The Seventh Circuit's order, though not a final judgment in the underlying 
appeal, is immediately enforceable as to Applicant and warrants this Court's 
interlocutory supervisory intervention to uphold the integrity of the judicial 
process.

iii
PARTIES TO THE PROCEEDING
Applicant: Katherine A. London, an attorney admitted to the bar of the 
Seventh Circuit and representing Plaintiff-Applicant Raymond E. Butler II in 
the underlying appeal.
Respondent: United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit. They
have been served pursuant to Rule 29.
RELATED PROCEEDINGS 
United States District Court (N.D. Ill.): 
Butler v. Eddi et. al., No. 1:25-cv-04443 (various dates in 2025) (underlying 
district court proceedings, including denial of disqualification motion against 
Judge Alexakis) 
United States District Court (W.D. Mich.): 
Butler v. Eddi et. al., No. 2:24-cv-00134 (various dates in 2024) (original district 
court proceedings transferred to N.D. Ill.) United States Court of Appeals (7th 
Cir.): 
Butler v. Eddi et. al., No. 25-2589 (Sept. 24, 2025) (motion to disqualify Judge 
Maldonado) 
Butler v. Eddi et. al., No. 25-2589 (Oct. 3, 2025) (denial of disqualification 
motion) 
Butler v. Eddi et. al., No. 25-2589 (Oct. 10, 2025) (order to show cause for 
sanctions) 
Butler v. Eddi et. al., No. 25-2589 (Oct. 20, 2025) (response to order to show 
cause) 
Butler v. Eddi et. al., No. 25-2589 (Nov. 7, 2025) (sanction order imposing $750 
fine, public reprimand, and referral to ARDC)

1
In the Supreme Court of the United States
───────────
No. 25__
KATHERINE A. LONDON, ESQ., APPLICANT
v.
 UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS FOR THE SEVENTH CIRCUIT
───────────
APPLICATION TO VACATE THE ORDER ISSUED
BY THE UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS FOR THE SEVENTH 
CIRCUIT AND REQUEST FOR AN IMMEDIATE ADMINISTRATIVE 
STAY
───────────
Applicant, Katherine A. London, Esq., respectfully submits this application,
pursuant to Rules 22 and 23 of the Rules of this Court and the All Writs Act, 28 
U.S.C. § 1651. Applicant respectfully requests vacatur of the Sanction Order issued 
by the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit on November 7, 2025, 
in Case No. 25-2589 (Butler v. Eddi et. al.), which imposes a $750 fine payable to 
the Clerk of Court within 30 days (due December 7, 2025) and serves as a public 
reprimand. Alternatively, Applicant requests an immediate administrative stay to 
preserve the status quo, as the fine became due on December 7, 2025, and 
enforcement, combined with the judicial referral to the Attorney Registration and 
Disciplinary Commission (ARDC) of the Illinois Supreme Court, continues to cause 
irreparable harm not only to Applicant but also presents an ongoing risk to the

2
representation of my client, Raymond E. Butler II, in the underlying case as well as
intolerable risks to the lives and safety of elderly patients residing in nursing homes 
owned by the Trusts in the underlying case while this Court considers the 
application. 
This sanction arises from zealous advocacy by Applicant in disqualification 
motions, which the Seventh Circuit deemed "scurrilous and unfounded" without 
sufficient evidentiary support or due process. The order is not final as to the 
underlying appeal but is immediately enforceable as to Applicant, warranting 
interlocutory review. Applicant intends to file a petition for writ of certiorari or 
mandamus and a brief promptly to challenge the order on grounds including abuse of 
discretion, violation of First Amendment rights, and misapplication of Federal Rule 
of Appellate Procedure 46. Vacatur is warranted, or a stay is necessary to prevent 
enforcement pending this Court's review.
The sanction order of the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh 
Circuit, issued on November 7, 2025, in Case No. 25-2589 (Butler v. Eddi, et al.), is 
reproduced at Attachment E. The order imposes a $750 fine, a public reprimand, 
and referral to the Attorney Registration and Disciplinary Commission (ARDC) of 
the Illinois Supreme Court. No prior opinions from the Seventh Circuit or the 
district court directly address the cause for the sanctions, but simply that they arise 
from motions filed in the underlying appeal of the denial of a motion for injunctive

3
relief for multiple injunctions in the Northern District of Illinois Case No. 1:25-cv04443.
STATEMENT
This application arises from multiple federal actions exposing an alleged 
racketeering enterprise under the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations 
Act (RICO), 18 U.S.C. § 1961 et seq. It further seeks vacatur or a stay of the Seventh 
Circuit's November 7, 2025, sanction order imposed on Applicant, in the appeal 
captioned Butler v. Eddi et. al., No. 25-2589. The order requires Applicant to pay a 
$750 fine within 30 days, issues a public reprimand, and forwards a copy to the 
Attorney Registration and Disciplinary Commission of the Illinois Supreme Court 
(ARDC) for potential further action (Attachment E). The sanctions stem from 
Applicant's filing of a motion to disqualify Circuit Judge Nancy L. Maldonado—in an 
underlying interlocutory appeal in a RICO action alleging widespread fraud, 
conversion of trust(s) assets resulting in elder abuse by a network of nursing home 
operators (Case No. 1:25-cv-04443) (Attachment A).
This case unveils a chilling escalation of harassment and intimidation tactics 
against Applicant, commencing almost immediately upon her involvement and 
intensifying throughout the litigation, thereby imperiling her, her family and her 
clients' safety, and making it difficult to fulfill her professional duties. Once 
Applicant filed her appearance in the underlying case, strangers in unmarked, 
blacked-out SUVs began surveilling the Applicant’s residence—driving past

4
multiple times daily, with individuals exiting vehicles to loiter menacingly in 
front—actions that have only grown more brazen as the case has progressed. 
Applicant has sustained repeated breach attempts to her home server, which 
contains not only personal information such as financial records but also her law 
practice data and the data owned by her husband’s business. The breaches are 
known as “brute force” attempts, meaning someone systematically tries countless 
password combinations—automated and relentless—until one cracks the server's 
defenses. It's not clever; these are voluminous, mass attacks, akin to picking a lock 
with every pin you own. The result is that the server demands ongoing upkeep to 
safeguard its stored data. Further, escalation has included interference in
Applicant’s home alarm system, “Fi” system for the family dogs, and vehicle 
navigation systems. 
The profoundly troubling and escalating pattern of harassment, stalking, 
cybersecurity breaches, and property damage directed at the Applicant throughout 
the pendency of these proceedings is nothing short of criminal. Applicant has added 
additional security measures at her home, including multiple cameras and mobile 
surveillance units with a “talk down” feature. This feature allows the now-employed
monitoring center to talk to trespassers via a loudspeaker and alert police to 
unauthorized activity. Further, the local Sheriff’s Office has placed marked vehicles 
outside Applicant's residence and added extra patrols to attempt to capture the 
offending parties. These security additions do not come without substantial

5
financial and emotional cost. Applicant has grave concerns for her family and pets, 
who reside with her. 
Applicant initially entered her appearance in Case No. 25-cv-04443 as local 
counsel for The Michigan Law Firm, following a sua sponte change of venue from 
Michigan to the Northern District of Illinois. Yet, amid this litigation, she has 
endured sustained and orchestrated threats that not only jeopardize the lives and 
safety of herself and her family, even within the sanctity of the courtroom, but also 
systematically undermines her capacity to zealously advocate for her client. 
Intensifying this external peril, conduct by federal judges has not only failed to 
mitigate but has actively exacerbated the threats, fostering an environment where 
courtroom improprieties spill over into real-world dangers, undermining the sanctity 
of the judicial process and eroding public confidence in the rule of law.
Compounding this injustice, counsel for the defendants in the parallel Illinois 
state action (Case No. 2022CH00675) have continually delayed discovery, while 
simultaneously, in the federal forum, some of those same attorneys demand a stay 
contingent upon the state case's outcome. As a result, both proceedings languish in 
limbo, with no meaningful discovery or depositions conducted after nearly four years 
of litigation, thereby perpetuating a cycle of delay that callously dismisses or denies 
the persistent dangers confronting the Applicant as well as the tens of thousands of 
nursing home residents under the defendant/trustees in the underlying case. This

6
Court must intervene to safeguard the elderly and disabled patients who are some of 
the collateral victims in the underlying RICO case, for the integrity of the judicial 
process, and to protect those who serve it.
For Applicant, this pattern of activity escalated on or about July 30, 2025, when 
The Michigan Law Firm filed an ex parte emergency motion to vacate the stay and 
protective order, freeze trust assets, and appoint a neutral fiduciary in the underlying 
RICO case (Case No. 1:25-cv-04443) critical relief sought after an illicit transfer of 
$544 million worth of commercial property (skilled nursing facilities) to preserve 
justice amid ongoing perils during the pendency of this litigation. Yet, District Judge 
Alexakis, via her Deputy Clerk, appeared to attempt to subvert due process by 
insisting on improper ex parte phone communications and evading a substantive 
ruling, instead pressuring counsel through emails to abandon the ex parte nature and 
consent to a hearing. The Applicant’s inquiries at 2:36 PM and 3:00 PM CST for 
clarification on the motion's status were met with coercive tactics, culminating in the 
judge's outright disregard of the emergency filing and compelling the Applicant to 
lodge a Notice of Appeal at 6:30 PM CST. 
Alarmingly, IP addresses from the Administrative Office of the United States 
Courts reveal access to Applicant’s biography page on her law firm website at 3:15 
PM and 8:04 PM CST on July 30, 2025, precisely during the exchanges with the 
District Court and post-Notice of Appeal (Attachment H). After the Notice of Appeal

7
was filed, Judge Alexakis failed to transmit it to the Appellate Court, preventing the 
assignment of a docketing number and preventing the emergency petition from the 
Applicant from being filed. On August 1, 2025, Applicant contacted the 7th Circuit 
Court of Appeals Clerk's Office to inquire whether a notice of appeal had been 
transmitted to the Appellate court to file the emergency petition. The Clerks informed 
Applicant that the Notice of Appeal and short record had not yet been sent over, but 
they would request it from the Northern Illinois District Clerks on an expedited basis 
and would notify Applicant via phone when the appeal was docketed. In the interim, 
information relayed to Applicant before docketing occurred indicated that Judge 
Alexakis contacted the Appellate Court clerk’s office four times, appearing to 
interfere with the appeal’s processing and potentially delaying justice. 
Shortly after docketing, IP addresses traced to the United States Court of 
Appeals accessed the Applicants' biography page on her law firm website on August 
1, 2025, at 3:20 PM CST, during the emergency petitions critical review period. An 
unsigned order denying the petition was promptly filed. This appears to show that 
the evaluation of the petition may have been based on the attorney who filed it, rather 
than the merits of the pleading. 
That petition, filed at 2:29 PM on August 1, was suspiciously denied by 4:03 PM. 
This review, if based on information obtained from Applicant law firm website 
attorney profile page, obstructed the appellate process, violated the requirement for

8
fair adjudication, and breached the Applicant-Appellant’s First Amendment right to 
petition and Fourteenth Amendment rights to due process and equal protection.
On August 4, 2025, at 12:16 PM CST, the Appellate Court, apparently under 
Maldonado, Brennan, and Hamilton, but with orders issued solely “By the Court” and 
lacking any judges' names or signatures, ordered the Applicant to file a brief on 
jurisdiction by August 18, 2025. A Motion for rehearing en banc was filed thereafter 
at 3:08 PM CST. At 4:16 PM CST, and access by IP addresses used by the Court of 
Appeals to the Applicant’s law firm website profile were logged on August 4, 2025, 
after the filing of a motion for an en banc hearing.
On August 6, 2025, the en banc motion submitted by Applicant was summarily 
denied, and the entire appeal was dismissed for lack of jurisdiction at 9:06 AM CST 
without briefing as previously ordered by the court, suggesting the court may have 
considered the en banc motion as Applicant’s response without due process. This left 
jurisdictional obligations unresolved, reflecting a possible effort to hinder the appeal 
and favor opposing parties. On August 7, 2025, District Judge Alexakis issued an 
order, erroneously stating that the Seventh Circuit had dismissed Appeal No. 25-
2315 on August 6, 2025, for lack of jurisdiction, thereby permitting injunctive relief
to be heard in the District Court on August 27, 2025. This assertion was incorrect, as 
the Appellate Court's mandate restoring jurisdiction was not issued until August 28,

9
2025. Nonetheless, Judge Alexakis proceeded to conduct a hearing on August 27, 
2025, exceeding the court's authority at that time.
In her order, Judge Alexakis improperly managed a motion by non-party CIBC 
Bank USA to enforce a protective order by treating the Applicant’s motion to strike 
as a response and instructing CIBC to file a reply by August 14, 2025. This procedural 
error disadvantaged the Applicant’s client by curtailing Applicant’s opportunities to 
object. Further, on August 8, 2025, the judge granted the defendants' motion to 
reschedule hearings on Applicant’s motions for default judgments from August 22 to 
August 27, 2025, extending similar delays to additional Applicant’s motions. These 
adjustments impeded Applicant’s progress for her client while permitting defendants' 
motions to advance without hindrance, reflecting unequal treatment under the law 
and contravening the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, as no 
comparable accommodations were afforded to Applicant.
On August 26, 2025, Applicant complied with Judge Alexakis's standing order 
regarding a 24-hour notice of WebEx appearances by contacting the Judge’s Deputy 
Clerk at 9:59 AM CST and emailing a request to appear remotely for the August 27 
hearing, citing escalated safety concerns. Website traffic records from the United 
States Courts indicate accesses to Applicant’s biography page on her law firm website 
at 10:39 AM CST, 11:29 AM CST, and 12:00 PM CST on August 26, and 10:16 AM 
CST during the August 27 hearing. These accesses, occurring in the context of her

10
expressed safety concerns, raise questions about judicial impartiality and potentially 
chill speech through erosion of an unbiased tribunal.
During the August 27, 2025, hearing on Applicant’s Motion to Vacate Stay, 
Protective Order, and Appoint a Neutral Fiduciary, Judge Alexakis interrogated
Applicant, on the record for approximately twenty minutes, regarding her WebEx 
request and the underlying safety threats, demanding details including the names of 
officers and police departments responding to calls for help when suspicious activity 
occurred outside her home. Further Alexakis made inquiries into attorney-client 
communications and commented on her competency to represent her client without 
an in-person appearance, such as asking whether she had discussed her ability to 
serve effectively with her client. These interactions coincided with ongoing incidents 
at Applicant residence, which have further impacted her representation.
On August 28, 2025, Judge Alexakis entered an order denying all Applicant’s 
motions while granting all defense motions, relying on a record that omitted certain 
facts and involved interpretations warranting review for fairness. Judge Alexakis 
also ordered Applicant to submit law enforcement reports concerning her safety 
threats by the end of the day, a requirement unrelated to the merits. When Applicant 
requested redactions to the names of police departments and other identifiers that 
would expose the location of her residence, the request was denied. Of particular 
note, around 1:00 AM CST on August 28, an unknown individual entered Applicant’s

11
residential property and severed her internet cable; although repaired the following 
day, the cable was cut again on August 30 and discarded in nearby bushes, further 
substantiating Applicant’s concern for the safety of her and her family. 
Additionally, procedural lapses in the district court's handling of Applicant's 
notices of appeal, leading to duplicative appellate dockets, have impeded efficient 
resolution and fairness, in contravention of Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure 
(FRAP) 3(d). On September 2, 2025, the district court transmitted the record, 
including a Notice of Appeal, to the appellate court around 8:30 AM CST, while 
Applicant concurrently filed an Amended Notice of Appeal to refine the appeal's scope 
and promptly contacted the appellate clerk, who confirmed transmission of the 
original but assured separate handling of the Amended Notice, with redundancy to 
be addressed by a jurisdictional attorney. By approximately 2:30 PM CST, however, 
the appellate court docketed Appeal No. 25-2529 solely on the original Notice, as the 
district court, despite awareness of the Amended Notice, neither promptly 
transmitted it nor notified the appellate court, fostering jurisdictional confusion.
From September 2 through 10, 2025, Applicant diligently pursued expedited 
transmission of the notice of appeal via repeated communications with district court 
clerks, who escalated the matter internally, yet the district court delayed action for 
nearly ten days, permitting opposing counsel to enter appearances and advance in 
the premature Appeal No. 25-2529. On September 10, 2025, the district court finally

12
transmitted the Amended Notice, docketed as Appeal No. 25-2589—the operative 
appeal intended to supersede the prior one—while an unsigned appellate order that 
same day directed Applicant to file a memorandum justifying retention of No. 25-
2529, a request Applicant declined based on prior clerical assurances of sua sponte 
resolution. On September 18, 2025, notwithstanding the docketing of the operative 
Appeal No. 25-2589, an appellate court order, again issued anonymously without 
judicial attribution, directed Applicant to file a docketing statement in the nonoperative Appeal No. 25-2529, evidencing what appeared to be intentional 
maintenance of parallel proceedings and bias in favor of prolonging confusion to the 
detriment of Applicant.
On September 24, 2025, an appellate court order, issued without judicial 
signature, initials, or clerk's signature, directed Applicant to file a docketing 
statement in Appeal No. 25-2589. On the same date, Applicant complied by filing the 
docketing statement in No. 25-2589, which included an explanation of the 
jurisdictional overlap and the superseding nature of the Amended Notice. 
Concurrently, Applicant filed a Motion to Disqualify Judge Maldonado in No. 25-2589
on behalf of her client, citing prior involvement and potential bias as grounds for 
recusal under 28 U.S.C. § 455(a) and (b). The motion included a Certificate of Good 
Faith and supporting affidavit from Applicant’s client, Raymond E. Butler, II, 
averring bias from extrajudicial sources. All allegations were grounded in court 
records and public documents.

13
September 25, 2025: An appellate court order, again anonymously issued, 
critiqued Applicant's docketing statement in No. 25-2589 for purported deficiencies, 
including failure to specify the appeal's filing date, elaborate on jurisdictional bases 
beyond final judgments, and clarify why the appeal from the injunction denial was 
not merely interlocutory. On October 2, 2025, in response to the September 25 order, 
Applicant filed an amended docketing statement in No. 25-2589 to address the 
deficiencies.
On October 3, 2025, Judge Maldonado denied Applicant's Motion to Disqualify, 
failing to recuse herself, without explanation, despite the motion's allegations of bias 
and her ongoing involvement in the case. Demonstrating further partiality, the denial 
order was filed in both Appeal No. 25-2529 and 25-2589, even though the motion was 
submitted exclusively in the operative No. 25-2589 case. This cross-filing exacerbated 
procedural chaos and evidenced disregard for the superseding appeal. On that same 
date, an appellate court order, again issued anonymously, sua sponte required 
Applicant to show cause for non-compliance with the September 10, 2025, order in 
No. 25-2529 regarding the dismissal memorandum. This action ignored the operative 
status of No. 25-2589 and Applicant's reasonable reliance on the clerk's assurances.
However, on that same date in a separate order in No. 25-2529, Judge Maldonado 
threatened sanctions against Applicant, including a $100 fine, for failure to file a 
docketing statement in the non-operative appeal. This threat constituted overt bias 
in favor of opposing counsel, who had filed in No. 25-2529, and against Applicant, as

14
it penalized reliance on the proper docket and perpetuated the district court's initial 
transmission errors.
Adding insult to injury, on October 10, 2025, the Court issued an unsigned 
show cause order (lacking any judge's name, signature, or initials) in Appeal No. 25-
2589, directing Applicant to respond to potential sanctions under FRAP 46(c) for 
alleged "conduct unbecoming a member of the bar." (Attachment C) The order 
ostensibly focused on the disqualification motion's language but referenced broader 
"scurrilous and unfounded accusations" against Judge Maldonado, implicitly drawing 
from the RICO complaint cited therein. This marked the beginning of the Court's
expansion beyond the motion itself.
A timely response to the show cause order was filed, addressing the allegations, 
denying misconduct, and requesting a hearing to present testimony and evidence “if 
necessary,” meaning, if the Court decided to impose sanctions (Attachment D). 
Applicant emphasized that the disqualification motion was protected advocacy under 
the First Amendment and 28 U.S.C. § 455, and that any reference to the RICO action 
was a legitimate ground for recusal (e.g., conflict of interest). No hearing was granted, 
violating Applicant’s due process requirements under In re Ruffalo, 390 U.S. 544 
(1968) (attorneys facing discipline entitled to notice and opportunity to defend).
The Court issued an unsigned and unattributable sanctions order on 
November 7, 2025, (again lacking any judge's name, signature, or initials), imposing 
a $750 fine, a public reprimand, and referral to the ARDC for further discipline.

15
Critically, while the order purported to sanction Applicant for the disqualification 
motion's "disrespect" and "knowingly misrepresented facts," it didn’t appear to rely 
on the motion itself. Specifically, the order referenced "evidence" of the undersigned’s
"unwillingness to take responsibility for her actions” and “continuing to present 
unsupported allegations denigrating Judge Maldonado’s conduct and character,” 
considered part of a pattern of "scurrilous and unfounded accusations," allegedly 
linking the undersigned’s alleged conduct to a prior motion to Disqualify Judge 
Alexakis in the same underlying case (1:25-cv-04443).
Applicant was denied a hearing, and a motion for rehearing, and on November 
16, 2025, the filed motion for en banc hearing on the Motion to Disqualify Judge 
Maldonado was also denied, all in unsigned and unattributable orders lacking any 
judge's name, signature, initials, or clerk’s initials, perpetuating harm (Attachments
F and G). 
On November 13, 2025, the Attorney Registration and Disciplinary 
Commission (ARDC) received a referral from the Seventh Circuit and sent Applicant
a letter seeking details regarding allegations of "judicial activism" and "lawfare" as 
discussed in the sanctions order, which extends beyond the disqualification motion
(Attachments I and J). This sequence of seemingly retaliatory actions stemming from 
the underlying RICO action, resulting in sanctions and now prompting potential 
reciprocal disbarment, impedes Applicant’s capacity to practice law effectively and 
represent her client in underlying concurrent state and federal proceedings, where

16
opposing counsel has introduced the sanctions order to challenge professional 
standing and credibility. This Court should grant relief to preserve due process, 
safeguard First Amendment protections for advocacy, and ensure unimpeded access 
to the courts.
On November 30, 2025, as Applicant boarded a car service from home for a 
scheduled House Judiciary briefing in Washington, a black SUV with darkened glass 
parked curbside, staring while she, her husband, and their two dogs waved farewell. 
It tailed her block-by-block; after the attorney signaled the driver to loop twice, it 
stayed locked on, then peeled off once a second tail took over. Back at the house, that 
first car circled slowly, scanning for her husband—circling again and again while the 
attorney was in flight. This isn't a coincidence; it's targeted surveillance that proves 
the threats aren't theory, and why the Court must step in now.
ARGUMENT
I. Applicant Is Likely To Succeed On The Merits 
A. The Seventh Circuit's Sanction Order Violates The First 
Amendment And Due Process By Punishing Zealous 
Advocacy 
The Seventh Circuit's sanctions violate fundamental constitutional 
protections and exceed its authority under Fed. R. App. P. 46, presenting questions 
of national importance meriting certiorari.

17
First, the sanctions infringe Applicant's First Amendment rights by 
punishing protected speech, and the national implications amplify the merits. The 
underlying RICO action addresses elder abuse in nursing homes, affecting tens of 
thousands of patients nationwide. Defendants’ enterprise involves significant fraud 
leading to substandard care and deaths. Sanctioning Applicant for challenging 
judicial impartiality in such cases sets a dangerous precedent, deterring attorneys 
from pursuing justice for vulnerable populations. This Court has recognized the 
need to protect advocacy in public-interest litigation. See NAACP v. Button, 371 
U.S. 415, 429 (1963) (First Amendment protects litigation as a form of political 
expression). Applicant’s success on certiorari is likely, as the sanctions impinge on 
core constitutional protections. 
Motions to disqualify judges, when based on reasonable grounds, are core 
advocacy protected from retaliation. See Dennis v. United States, 341 U.S. 494, 513 
(1951) (attorneys have a duty to raise ethical concerns). The Seventh Circuit labeled 
Applicant's arguments "scurrilous and unfounded" without due process or an 
evidentiary hearing, violating the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments. See In re 
Snyder, 472 U.S. 634, 645 (1985) (sanctions for "conduct unbecoming" must be 
narrowly tailored and supported by evidence). No specific examples of “scurrilous 
and/or unfounded” accusations were presented, no hearing was held, a motion for 
rehearing was denied, and the order mischaracterizes the disqualification motion as 
unfounded, ignoring cited evidence of judicial irregularities.

18
Further, the sanctions conflict with this Court's precedents on attorney 
discipline. Rule 46 requires "conduct inimical to the administration of justice," but 
Applicant's filings adhered to the Seventh Circuit's Standards for Professional 
Conduct by raising good-faith concerns about bias and including a signed affidavit 
from the Plaintiff-Applicant, Raymond E. Butler II. Punishing such advocacy chills 
attorneys nationwide from challenging judicial misconduct, undermining public trust 
in the judiciary.
Additionally, Certiorari is likely because this case implicates a circuit split on 
the scope of appellate sanctions for disqualification motions. Compare Seventh 
Circuit's broad application here with more restrained approaches in other circuits 
(e.g., Ninth Circuit requiring clear evidence of bad faith). The national implications 
are profound: If upheld, these sanctions will deter attorneys from exposing RICO 
enterprises in critical sectors like nursing homes, where defendants' fraud and 
neglect cause thousands of deaths annually. Federal data shows over 200,000 nursing 
home residents die yearly from preventable causes like neglect; the underlying cases 
seek to hold accountable operators whose facilities have faced penalties for 
substandard care. Silencing advocates perpetuates this crisis, affecting vulnerable 
populations across all 50 states.

19
The Seventh Circuit’s sanctions punish protected speech and zealous 
advocacy in violation of the First Amendment. Attorneys have a constitutional right 
to criticize judges and advocate vigorously for their clients, so long as their 
statements are not knowingly false or made with reckless disregard for the truth. 
See Gentile v. State Bar of Nev., 501 U.S. 1030, 1051 (1991) (plurality opinion) 
(attorney speech is protected unless it poses a substantial likelihood of material 
prejudice); In re Snyder, 472 U.S. 634, 647 (1985) (overturning sanctions for 
attorney criticism of court as "conduct unbecoming"). 
Here, Applicant’s disqualification motions were based on reasonable beliefs 
about potential bias, derived from the judges’ rulings, affiliations, and conduct in the 
underlying case. The motions cited specific concerns, such as ideological bias and 
misconduct, which Applicants attorney asserted in good faith to protect her client’s 
due process rights under 28 U.S.C. § 455. These were not "scurrilous and unfounded" 
as the Seventh Circuit claimed, but rather expressions of advocacy grounded in 
ethical duties. See Model Rules of Prof’l Conduct r. 3.1 (Am. Bar Ass’n 2023) 
(permitting good-faith arguments for modification of law). Punishing such filings 
chills First Amendment rights and undermines the adversarial system. 
Moreover, the Seventh Circuit's issuance of multiple unsigned orders 
throughout the sanction process—including the October 10, 2025, show cause order, 
the November 7, 2025, sanction order, and the denial of en banc review—constitutes 
procedural irregularities that violate fundamental principles of transparency,

20
accountability, and due process. These orders lack any judge's name, signature, or 
initials, obscuring the decision-makers and suggesting potential undue influence by 
Judge Maldonado, who has a direct conflict as a named defendant in the related RICO 
action (Butler v. Alexakis, et al., No. 1:25-cv-10904). This anonymity contravenes the 
Code of Conduct for United States Judges (Canon 2, requiring avoidance of 
impropriety and its appearance) and exacerbates the due process deficiencies under 
In re Ruffalo, 390 U.S. 544 (1968), by denying Applicant the ability to identify and 
challenge biased adjudicators. Such practices, while perhaps common for routine 
procedural matters, are inappropriate in attorney disciplinary proceedings where 
personal accountability is essential, further demonstrating the Court's abuse of 
discretion and warranting reversal.
Further, the sanctions violate due process by punishing without adequate 
notice or opportunity to be heard. Fed. R. App. P. 46 requires "conduct unbecoming," 
but the Seventh Circuit applied a vague standard from its internal guidelines, failing 
to specify how Applicant’s filings knowingly misrepresented facts. The show-cause 
order and response process was perfunctory, denying Applicant a hearing. See 
Roadway Express, Inc. v. Piper, 447 U.S. 752, 767 (1980) (due process requires notice 
and hearing before attorney sanctions). This procedural deficiency compounds the 
substantive error, as the sanctions rest on a mischaracterization of Applicant’s goodfaith advocacy as misconduct.

21
B. The Allegations In The Disqualification Motions Were WellFounded And Protected By Professional Standards 
The Seventh Circuit erred in deeming Applicant’s allegations "unsupported" 
and "denigrating." The motions were supported by evidence from the record, 
including the judges’ rulings that appeared to favor defendants despite strong claims 
of fraud and abuse. For instance, the disqualification motion against Judge 
Maldonado cited a pattern of decisions that Applicant reasonably believed 
demonstrated bias, coupled with IP logs showing Applicant’s law firm website profile 
page accessed during the pendency of critical motions and consistent with prior 
criticisms of the court. Such allegations are protected under professional standards, 
which require attorneys to raise disqualification issues when bias is suspected. See 
28 U.S.C. § 455(a) (requiring disqualification for appearance of impartiality); Liteky 
v. United States, 510 U.S. 540, 555 (1994) (bias claims must be evaluated on facts). 
Applicant attorney’s response to the show-cause order reiterated these grounds 
without evasion, demonstrating accountability rather than the "lack of responsibility" 
the court alleged. The sanctions also overlook the broader context: a RICO enterprise 
with national reach, where defendants’ control of skilled nursing facilities has led to 
documented harms. Public records and complaints (e.g., from state health 
departments) substantiate the underlying claims of elder deaths due to neglect. By 
sanctioning Applicant, the Seventh Circuit effectively shields this enterprise, 
violating Applicant’s—and the public’s—right to access the courts. See Christopher v. 
Harbury, 536 U.S. 403, 415 (2002) (access to courts is a fundamental right).

22
This Court is likely to reverse, as the sanctions exceed the bounds of Rule 46 
and infringe on protected advocacy. See In re Snyder, supra, at 645 (Rule 46 
encompasses only conduct showing "unfitness," not mere criticism). 
II. Irreparable Harm Absent Vacatur
Without vacatur or a stay, Applicant continues to endure immediate and 
irreparable harm. The $750 fine is past due, but more critically, the public reprimand 
and ARDC referral for possible suspension or disbarment will continue to inflict 
irreparable harm, and irreversible inflict lasting damage. See Hollingsworth v. Perry, 
558 U.S. 183, 190 (2010) (reputational harm from public sanctions is irreparable). 
The reprimand has been published, and the order has been included by opposing 
counsel in multiple motions, suggesting Applicant is incapable of practicing law 
honestly and ethically, thus harming Applicant's professional standing and client 
relationships. Further, the ARDC referral could lead to suspension or disbarment, 
preventing Applicant from continuing the underlying RICO cases.
This harm extends nationally: Applicant’s client claims uncover systemic 
skilled nursing facility abuses by the defendants, whose enterprise spans multiple 
states and involves substantial fraud leading to excessive resident deaths. Tens of 
thousands of elderly and disabled individuals in defendant-held or operated facilities 
face ongoing risks of neglect, abuse, and premature death due to defendants' 
unchecked behavior. If Applicant is sidelined, these cases will continue to stall,

denying justice and allowing preventable fatalities to continue. Federal oversight 
(e.g., via HHS and CMS) is insufficient without private enforcement; sanctions here 
set a precedent deterring other attorneys, exacerbating a public health crisis affecting 
over 1.4 million nursing home residents nationwide.
No adequate remedy exists without a stay, as monetary compensation cannot 
restore reputation or prevent deaths.
III. The Balance Of Equities Weighs Strongly In Favor Of The 
Applicant 
The equities favor a vacatur or stay. Respondent (the Seventh Circuit) suffers 
no harm from a temporary pause in enforcing the sanctions, as the order’s purpose of 
deterring misconduct can be achieved post-review if upheld. In contrast, Applicant
faces immediate financial ($750 fine), continued reputational, and professional harm,
including possible suspension or disbarment with ripple effects on public justice. 
The public interest strongly supports vacatur: protecting a vulnerable 
population from nursing home abuse outweighs enforcing sanctions on advocacy. 
Tens of thousands of residents nationwide depend on such litigation for 
accountability. See 18 U.S.C. § 1961 et seq. (RICO aimed at combating organized 
fraud). Equity demands preserving the status quo to avoid injustice.

Further, upholding attorneys' rights to challenge bias promotes judicial 
integrity and access to justice. Conversely, allowing these sanctions fosters a culture 
of intimidation, particularly in cases exposing elder abuse. The national nursing 
home crisis—marked by high mortality rates from neglect (e.g., 15-20% annual death 
rates in substandard facilities)—demands robust legal challenges. Defendants' 
alleged conduct has led to documented injustices; staying the sanctions ensures 
accountability, potentially saving lives and serving the broader interest in protecting 
vulnerable populations.
IV. The Issues Raised By The Order Warrant Certiorari 
Certiorari is warranted because the Seventh Circuit’s order raises significant 
questions about the limits of attorney speech and sanctions in federal courts. This 
Court has frequently granted review in cases involving attorney discipline that 
implicates First Amendment rights. See, e.g., Gentile, supra; In re Snyder, supra. The 
order creates a circuit split: some circuits require clear evidence of bad faith for 
sanctions under Rule 46 (see, e.g., In re Palmisano, 70 F.3d 483, 487 (7th Cir. 1995) 
(requiring hearing)), while others apply a more deferential standard. The national 
implications—chilling advocacy for plaintiffs in financial fraud cases and skilled 
nursing facility victims—affect interstate commerce and elder rights, areas of federal 
concern. See 42 U.S.C. § 1396 (federal nursing home standards).

At least four Justices are likely to vote for certiorari given the constitutional 
stakes and national implications to thousands of elderly nursing home patients.

III. LEGAL STANDARD
Under 28 U.S.C. § 455(a), a judge "shall disqualify himself in any proceeding 
in which his impartiality might reasonably be questioned." This objective 
standard protects the public's confidence in the judiciary (Liteky v. United
States, 510 U.S. 540, 548 (1994)). Section 455(b)(1) mandates recusal where the 
judge "has a personal bias or prejudice concerning a party."

 Judges are presumed impartial, and the burden is on the movant to present 
factual allegations sufficient to overcome this presumption. Allegations must be 
credible and based on facts, not conclusory statements. In re Maurice, 167 B.R. 
114, 125; United States v. Baskes, 687 F.2d 165, 170 (7th Cir. 1981). To 
disqualify a judge, the asserted bias or prejudice must be personal and arise 
from extrajudicial matters. Id.
 A party's lawsuit against a judge creates a per se conflict, as it places the 
judge in the adversarial position of defending against allegations of corruption 
and bias (see Preston v. United States, 923 F.2d 731, 22, 25 (2d Cir. 1991) 
(recusal mandatory when judge sued by party)). Extrajudicial factors, such as 
political ties or public criticisms, further taint impartiality (United States v. 
Murphy, 768 F.2d 1518, 1527 (7th Cir. 1985)).
The grounds asserted herein align with general principles for asserting 
appropriate grounds for disqualification, as reflected in codes such as the ABA 
Model Code of Judicial Conduct Rule 2.11 (requiring disqualification where 
impartiality might reasonably be questioned) and analogous provisions in 
administrative contexts (e.g., 28 C.F.R. § 76.16, providing for disqualification of 
administrative judges upon self-recognition of bias or party motion). These 
principles emphasize factual, non-conclusory allegations of bias from 
extrajudicial sources, which this motion provides through specific incidents and 
public records.

I. FACTUAL BACKGROUND
A. Legal Framework for Assessing Allegations in Disqualification Motions
Under federal law, motions for judicial disqualification must be evaluated against an 
objective standard that safeguards the integrity of judicial proceedings. Pursuant to 28 
U.S.C. §455(a), a judge shall disqualify herself in any proceeding where her impartiality 
might reasonably be questioned, and under §455(b)(1), disqualification is mandatory where 
personal bias or prejudice exists against a party. Complementing this, 28 U.S.C. §144 
requires that such motions be supported by an affidavit stating facts and reasons for belief in 
bias or prejudice, certified as made in good faith and not for delay.
The Supreme Court has clarified that allegations in disqualification motions must be 
"sufficiently definite and particular" to overcome the presumption of judicial impartiality, 
arising from extrajudicial sources rather than mere disagreement with rulings. Liteky v. 
United States, 510 U.S. 540, 555 (1994) (holding that bias must stem from sources outside 
the judicial proceeding, such as personal animus or extrajudicial conduct, and not from 
"opinions formed by the judge on the basis of facts introduced or events occurring in the 
course of the current proceedings"). See also United States v. Baskes, 687 F.2d 165, 170 
(7th Cir. 1981) (bias must be personal and extrajudicial, not inferred from judicial acts 
alone).
Scurrilous allegations are those intended to vilify or degrade without basis, often 
characterized by inflammatory language unsupported by evidence. In contrast, the Motion 
here aligns with the ABA Model Code of Judicial Conduct Rule 2.11 and analogous federal 
principles, which mandate disqualification based on factual, non-conclusory grounds from 
Case: 25-2589 Document: 28 Filed: 10/20/2025 Pages: 9

3
extrajudicial origins. The Motion satisfies these criteria through specific, documented 
assertions, thereby avoiding any characterization as scurrilous or unfounded.
B. Factual and Evidentiary Basis of the Motion's Allegations
The Motion's assertions are meticulously tethered to verifiable facts, court records, public 
documents, and extrajudicial evidence, as required by controlling authority. Far from being 
scurrilous, they are presented in a measured, professional manner, supported by crossreferences to exhibits, complaints, and public records, and certified under penalty of 
perjury. 
 The Motion asserts that Judge Maldonado's status as a named defendant in Butler v. 
Alexakis, et al., No. 1:25-cv-10904 (N.D. Ill.) (the "RICO Action") creates a per se conflict 
under §455(a), as it positions her as an adversary defending against claims of racketeering, 
obstruction of justice (18 U.S.C. § 1503), wire fraud (18 U.S.C. § 1343), and constitutional 
violations. This is not unfounded; it is directly predicated on the filed RICO Complaint 
which details specific acts. Such a lawsuit against a presiding judge inherently raises an 
appearance of partiality, as recognized in precedent like Preston v. United States, 923 F.2d 
731, 734 (9th Cir. 1991) (recusal mandatory when judge is sued by a party, placing her in an 
adversarial role).

A. The Filings Do Not Constitute Conduct Unbecoming or a Violation of Court 
Rules
Discipline under FRAP 46(c), requires clear evidence of bad faith, frivolousness, or intent 
to harass, not merely unsuccessful or aggressive advocacy. See In re Snyder, 472 U.S. 634, 
645 (1985) (conduct unbecoming involves moral turpitude or dishonesty); Roadway 
Express, Inc. v. Piper, 447 U.S. 752, 766 (1980) (bad faith required for sanctions). Here, the 
filings were made in good faith and do not warrant discipline.
First, the motion is grounded in factual allegations from Mr. Butler's affidavit and

against judge creates per se conflict).
B. The Motion is Protected by Absolute Litigation Privilege
 
 Litigation privilege refers to an absolute immunity that protects lawyers, clients, and 
sometimes third parties from civil liability (e.g., defamation, emotional distress, or fraud 
claims) for statements or communications made during judicial or quasi-judicial 
proceedings. The goal is to encourage open communication in litigation without fear of 
retaliatory lawsuits, avoiding a "chilling effect" on legal processes. The communications 
related to ongoing judicial proceedings or pre-litigation, if litigation is contemplated in 
good faith and under serious consideration, are included. The statement must have some 
relation to the proceeding, and the motive is irrelevant.
 In the Seventh Circuit, which applies Illinois substantive law to privilege claims in cases 
like this (arising from proceedings in the Northern District of Illinois), the absolute litigation 
privilege is broadly construed to shield "anything said or written in the course of a legal 
proceeding," provided it pertains to the litigation. See Joan M. Steffes v. Stepan Co., 144 F.3d 
1070, 1074 (7th. Cir. 1998) (holding that the privilege protects statements in pleadings, 
motions, and other court filings, even if potentially defamatory, as long as they bear some 
relation to the case). This doctrine, rooted in the Restatement (Second) of Torts §587, extends 
to "defamatory matter concerning another in communications preliminary to a proposed 
judicial proceeding, or in the institution of or during the course and as a part of, a judicial 
Case: 25-2589 Document: 28 Filed: 10/20/2025 Pages: 9

7
proceeding in which [the party] participates, if the matter has some relation thereto." The 
privilege is absolute, meaning it applies regardless of malice or falsity, to foster "unfettered 
expression" in the adversarial process. Thomas v. Petrulis, 465 N.E.2d 932, 934 (Ill. App. Ct. 
1984) (adopting Restatement principles).
 Here, every allegation in the Motion is directly tied to the disqualification grounds under 
28 U.S.C. §§455(a) and (b)(1). These statements were made in a formal appellate motion, 
supported by exhibits and pertain exclusively to the impartiality inquiry at issue in this appeal. 
They are not extraneous or gratuitous but essential to demonstrating extrajudicial bias from 
sources like exhibits in the RICO suit itself. As such, they fall squarely within the privilege's 
scope, barring any civil liability or derivative sanctions. See In re Sch. Asbestos Litig., 977 
F.2d 764, 776 (3d Cir. 1992) (applying similar principles to protect litigation-related 
statements from retaliatory claims).
 Federal courts, including the Seventh Circuit, routinely apply this state-law privilege in 
federal proceedings where, as here, the underlying claims involve state tort-like elements 
(e.g., defamation implied in "scurrilous" allegations). Imposing sanctions under Fed. R. App. 
P. 46 for such privileged statements would undermine the privilege's purpose, deterring 
attorneys from raising legitimate recusal issues and violating due process. See Chambers v. 
NASCO, Inc., 501 U.S. 32, 44 (1991) (courts' inherent sanction powers must yield to absolute 
immunities); see also Buckley v. Fitzsimmons, 20 F.3d 789 (7th Cir. 1994) (discussing limits 
on prosecutorial immunity but affirming absolute protection for in-court acts).

 Similarly, the Affidavit of Raymond E. Butler II avers personal knowledge of the

Discipline would chill advocacy for clients alleging judicial misconduct. See In re Maurice, 
167 B.R. 114, 125 (Bankr. N.D. Ill. 1994) (allegations must be credible but not proven for 
good faith).
If a hearing is necessary, undersigned counsel requests one to present additional evidence, 
including Mr. Butler's testimony.

advances credible, fact-based allegations derived from extrajudicial sources, as required by

Originating Case Information:

Northern District of Illinois, Eastern Division
District Judge Georgia N. Alexakis
The following are before the court:
1. PLAINTIFF-APPELLANT'S MOTION TO DISQUALIFY JUDGE NANCY 
L. MALDONADO, filed on September 24, 2025, by Attorney Katherine London.
2. REPLY IN RESPONSE TO ORDER TO SHOW CAUSE UNDER FED. R. APP. P. 46, filed on 
October 20, 2025, by Attorney Katherine London.
On September 24, 2025, appellant Raymond Butler—through his counsel, Katherine London—
filed a motion to disqualify Judge Maldonado, levying scurrilous and unfounded accusations of 
judicial misconduct and ideological bias. On October 3, 2025, Judge Maldonado denied the 
disqualification request, and on October 10, 2025, this court issued an order for Ms. London to 
show cause why she should not be sanctioned. In her response, Ms. London took no

No. 25-2589 Page 2
responsibility for her actions and continued to present unsupported allegations denigrating 
Judge Maldonado’s conduct and character. Ms. London’s lack of respect for members of the 
court is not isolated to this appeal—she filed a similar motion with similarly egregious 
allegations against Judge Alexakis in the district court, and she previously accused a panel of 
this court of engaging in “judicial activism” and “lawfare.” 
 
Under Rule 46 of the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure, we may suspend, disbar, or 
discipline a member of our bar “for conduct unbecoming a member of the bar.” Fed. R. App. P. 
46(b), (c). The Supreme Court has broadly construed the Rule to encompass “conduct contrary 
to professional standards that shows an unfitness to discharge continuing obligations to clients 
or the courts[] or conduct inimical to the administration of justice.” In re Snyder, 472 U.S. 634, 
645 (1985). 
 
Ms. London’s conduct—including her unwillingness to take responsibility for her actions—
meets that bar. This court’s standards of professional conduct require that all attorneys “speak 
and write civilly and respectfully in all communications with the court” and that they “not 
knowingly misrepresent, mischaracterize, misquote, or miscite facts … in any oral or written 
communication to the court.” Standards for Professional Conduct Within the Seventh Federal 
Judicial Circuit. Ms. London has repeatedly shown disrespect for members of this court and 
knowingly misrepresented facts in court filings.
 
Accordingly, IT IS ORDERED that attorney Katherine London shall pay a fine of $750 to the 
clerk of court within 30 days of this order. The clerk of court shall forward a copy of this order, 
which serves as a public reprimand, to the Attorney Registration and Disciplinary Commission 
of the Illinois Supreme Court for any action it deems appropriate. Further conduct of this nature 
could result in additional sanctions.
